---
title: "Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity"
---

Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label
without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

## 1. Is a tertiary amine charged?

Trimethylamine has three methyl groups on N. State its charge before and after accepting one proton.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
Neutral (CH₃)₃N has three N–C bonds and one lone pair. Its conjugate acid (CH₃)₃NH⁺ has four bonds and charge +1.
:::

## 2. Which pKa belongs in a basicity comparison?

Conjugate-acid pKa values are 10.7 for ethylammonium and 4.6 for anilinium. Which neutral base is stronger in comparable aqueous conditions?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
Ethylamine. Its conjugate acid is the weaker acid with larger pKa. Basicity is an equilibrium property and is not a universal nucleophilic-rate ranking.
:::

## 3. Is cyclohexane aromatic?

It is a six-membered ring. Explain why this is insufficient.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
It has no continuous cyclic p-orbital network. It is nonaromatic; being cyclic does not imply aromaticity or antiaromaticity.
:::

## 4. Which nitrogen pair is in the sextet?

Compare pyridine and pyrrole nitrogen lone pairs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
The pyridine lone pair lies outside its aromatic pi system. The pyrrole pair supplies two of the six aromatic pi electrons, making ordinary N protonation much less favourable.
:::

## 5. Does net zero mean no charge?

Draw glycine in its predominant form near pH 6 with supplied pKa values 2.3 and 9.6.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻ has N charge +1 and carboxylate charge −1, giving net zero. It is a zwitterion, not an entirely uncharged molecule.
:::

## 6. Is peptide nitrogen a simple amine?

Identify the neighbouring structural feature that changes its electron availability.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
Peptide nitrogen is directly attached to a carbonyl as part of an amide. Its pair delocalises into C=O, unlike the pair in a simple alkylamine.
:::
